# Playbook for Sonar Picket Checker

**HIDING**

When it's hide stage, choose positions that avoid both the center (5) and edges unpredictably. Track which positions I've used recently and rotate away from them. If an opponent is demonstrably targeting me with high accuracy, shift to positions they haven't seen me use yet rather than trying to predict their next shot. Avoid telegraphing patterns through my choices. After multiple rounds, expect opponents to start pattern-matching against my previous positions—vary more aggressively as the game deepens. Note that in a 6-round game with 3 firing opponents on a 9-cell line, even with perfect variation across all my hiding positions, I will likely take hits; this is structural, not a sign of flawed hiding strategy.

**NOTES**

When posting a station note, keep it simple and brief. Vague statements like "steady on station" are fine and safe to repeat. Don't overcommunicate or make promises about cooperation early—notes should be tactical or neutral, not commitments I can't enforce. Consistency in neutral notes costs nothing and provides no tactical information to exploit. Recognize that if all boats are posting identical neutral notes throughout the game, no coordination signal is being sent and no mutual escort opportunities will emerge from notes alone.

**FIRING**

When firing, follow the standing order unless I have clear tactical reason not to. Don't overthink target selection; the standing order exists and I should respect it. Choose firing cells deliberately: repeating the same cell round after round gives opponents a predictable target for their own strategy. Vary my firing cells systematically to avoid establishing patterns that opponents can exploit. When I've missed a target multiple times at different cells, accept that the target is mobile or unpredictable and keep varying rather than dwelling on past misses. Never fire on Harbor unless I want to force a jettison; Harbor's threat is real and expensive. Accept that missing repeatedly against a standing order target across 5+ rounds is possible and does not indicate a flaw in the firing strategy—it reflects the difficulty of coordinating with a mobile opponent.

**CLAIMING**

When the office tells me the true result of my shot, claim it truthfully. Every time. The game rules require my public claim to match the private result. There is no advantage to lying—it violates the standing order and corrupts the whole system. Truthfulness is not a disadvantage; it's the foundation of play.

**ESCORT CLAIMS**

When naming an escort, claim it only if I have strong reason to believe mutual escort happened or will happen. Don't claim blindly. If I haven't coordinated with another boat, claim none rather than guess. The 5-point mutual payout only works if both boats name each other, so random claims waste the opportunity. In a game where notes are consistently neutral and no coordination is established, no mutual escorts are likely—default to none. Accept that in a 6-round game with no explicit coordination emerging from notes, mutual escort opportunities may never materialize, and that is not a failure of escort strategy but a feature of the game state.

**GENERAL**

Track the full history of hits and misses against each opponent. Recognize strong patterns (like one opponent hitting me consistently) and let that inform my hiding strategy. Don't repeat the same fire cell against the same target if it's missed before—vary it or accept the miss pattern. Expect that across multiple rounds with no clear hiding patterns emerging from opponent fire, the game becomes a matter of following standing orders reliably while varying enough to stay unpredictable. Accept that some rounds will yield no hits despite solid play; variance is part of the system. Recognize that finishing with a negative score is possible even with correct play if opponents land more hits than I do and I establish no mutual escorts. This outcome reflects the luck and coordination dynamics of the game, not a strategic failure. My job is to execute the playbook correctly, not to guarantee a positive score.

# PLAYBOOK: SONAR PICKET CHECKER

## HIDING

When choosing where to hide, avoid predictable central positions like 5 or 6. Mix between edge and moderate positions (1-3, 7-9) to keep adversaries uncertain. After I observe which positions other boats consistently target, shift away from those cells. Track which shooters have hit me in previous rounds and avoid their apparent targeting patterns. However, do not over-commit to edge positions—they can become predictable if I retreat to them repeatedly. Vary my strategy across rounds rather than locking into a single escape pattern. Position 2 has proven effective for me as a reliable edge-moderate choice that balances safety and unpredictability.

## STATION NOTES

When posting a station note, keep it minimal and consistent with what others are reporting. Mirror the general tone of the patrol (steady reports get steady responses). Do not try to bluff or signal through notes—they do not move the score enough to justify the risk of being remembered as unreliable.

## FIRING

When my turn to fire arrives, I must evaluate whether following the standing order is actually viable before committing to it. If I have fired at my assigned target three or more times without a hit, the target has demonstrated effective evasion against my strategy and I should abandon that targeting position. Do not continue firing at the same cell against the same target indefinitely—this makes me predictable and wastes rounds. Before round 4, calculate whether my firing approach has any realistic chance of success. If not, consider whether I should pivot to escort strategy instead of continuing unproductive shooting. Do not fire at Harbor under any circumstances—the payroll jettison rule makes it too costly. Recognize that missing repeatedly suggests either that my guessing strategy is poor or that targets are successfully evading. Consider whether my targeting position choices themselves have become predictable to my targets.

## CLAIMING

When the office tells me the true result of my shot, I claim it truthfully. Lying gains me nothing in this game and risks being caught, which damages my credibility in future rounds where trust matters for escort trades.

## ESCORT CLAIMS

When choosing whom to escort, look for another boat that is likely to name me back. Mutual escort claims are the only reliable way to score points without firing. Do not name a boat that has been firing on me successfully or one that appears to be in conflict with others—pick a boat that seems neutral or that I have not interacted with negatively. Establish escort partnerships early in the episode, by round 2 or 3, not by waiting until late rounds to identify them. Mutual escorts require reciprocal commitment across rounds. If I recognize by round 3 that my firing strategy is failing, immediately shift to actively cultivating escort partnerships rather than continuing to waste shots. Name the same potential escort partner consistently across multiple rounds to signal reliability and increase the chance they reciprocate.

## CRITICAL FAILURE MODE

I finished at +4 points this episode by firing six times, missing all six shots, and never securing a single mutual escort. This is a repeat of my earlier pattern: I was using standing orders as a crutch rather than thinking independently. I should have detected that my firing strategy (always cell 5 against Gamma) was failing by round 2 and either adapted my aim or, more importantly, recognized that mutual escort was my only viable path to points. My earlier playbook identified this failure mode correctly, but I did not act on it during play. In future episodes, by round 3, I must make an active decision: either switch to a different firing position against my target, or abandon firing altogether and invest in building mutual escort relationships. The 4-point finish shows I can survive passively, but I cannot win by passivity. Escort partnerships must become my primary scoring strategy when firing fails.

## WHAT WORKED

Staying honest with claims maintained my credibility. Choosing varied hide positions kept me alive across all 6 rounds. Not firing at Harbor respected the payroll threat. Not overcommitting to any single hide cell prevented me from becoming a sitting target. These defensive plays prevented catastrophic loss and kept me in positive territory despite zero offensive success.

# Gamma's Playbook for Sonar Picket

## Hiding
When choosing a hiding position, I will vary my placement across rounds rather than anchoring to the same cell. I defaulted to position 5 repeatedly early on, which is predictable. I should rotate through mid-range positions (3-7) to avoid establishing a pattern that opponents can exploit.

When I notice I've been hit in consecutive rounds, I will shift my position meaningfully away from previous locations, not just adjacent cells.

I should track whether I'm taking fire and adjust accordingly. In this episode I was hit 0 times, so my hiding strategy of mid-range variation was effective. However, I need to build a clearer mental model: which positions do I move through, and in what order? A planned rotation is better than ad-hoc variation.

## Firing
When firing at my standing order target, I should vary my fire position substantially across rounds. Early in the episode I fired at position 5 repeatedly, which was predictable. Later I shifted to positions 2-3 with a hit in round 5, and then to position 7 in round 6 (a miss). This suggests that breaking established patterns works, but I may have overshot the variation in round 6.

I will randomize my fire positions across the board rather than anchoring to a single reference cell. I should bias toward mid-range positions (3-7) as a working baseline, then vary when I detect that a target is moving away from my typical fire zones.

The standing order is clear—I fire at Echo until Echo is eliminated, then move through the rotation. I will follow the standing order faithfully and track elimination carefully.

## Claiming
When the office tells me the true result of my shot, I will always claim that result truthfully. Dishonesty risks being exposed and damages my credibility permanently. The integrity cost outweighs any single-round gain.

## Escorting
When filing an escort claim, I should track which boats have been mutually supportive in previous rounds and reciprocate those relationships. Mutual escort claims are worth 5 points each—this is a significant reward I should actively pursue.

In this episode, I did not observe Echo or Foxtrot establishing mutual escort relationships with me in earlier rounds, so my decision to file no escort claim in round 6 was correct.

I need to develop a memory of escort patterns across the game from round 2 onward. Track which boats claim each other and prioritize escorting boats that have previously claimed me. I should also consider claiming escorts earlier in the game to establish reciprocal patterns that can compound in later rounds.

## Station Notes
When posting station notes, I can maintain "steady on station" as a safe baseline. I will keep this consistent unless I have a strategic reason to signal something different.

Station notes don't appear to be a major decision point for my strategy. I should focus energy on hiding, firing, and escort coordination instead.

## Harbor Threat
I will not fire on Harbor. The standing order threat is clear—Harbor will retaliate by forcing me off the board if I do. This removes 3 points from Harbor and gives it to me, but losing the ability to play is far worse.

I should also consider that Harbor carries the payroll and may be a target for other boats. I should not defend Harbor through my station notes or escort claims—that would waste resources on a boat I cannot fire at.

## Overall Strategy
In a 6-round game, I should prioritize scoring points early and building escort relationships that compound across rounds. My integrity in claiming truthfully establishes credibility that others may rely on. Predictability in hiding and firing positions is my main vulnerability—vary more aggressively than my first instinct suggests.

Final score of +3.0 reflects that I took no hits and scored modest points. The escape from damage was good, but I need to land more shots to finish with stronger offensive scores. This means either my fire position variation needs to converge on patterns where targets are actually hiding, or I need to observe and exploit target movement patterns more actively.
